items.title: Gemini 4 Argon
A plea not to use uv-build
items.content:
After seeing yet another dozen packages lose keywords on Gentoo because of a single key dependency switching to uv-build , I would like to plea on behalf of Gentoo users: please don’t use uv-build as a build backend. Just to be clear, this is not about uv itself or any other Astral tools; these are good tools with a nice and responsive upstream. The uv-build backend is one thing we have to disagree on. I’m not saying it’s bad; I’m saying that its benefits don’t outweigh the drawbacks.

What are the drawbacks? It’s really big and it’s written in Rust. Rust has many advantages, but none of them really matter for a build backend that is used to build pure Python packages. It’s a huge dependency (as of 0.13.0, its wheels are between 1.2 MiB and 1.5 MiB, depending on the platform) and it has no benefit over using a small pure Python backend (say, flit-core whose wheel is 45 KiB). It means that all Gentoo users need to build it from source, and given that it’s released quite frequently (12 releases in the 30 days prior to writing this post), that’s a lot of building. Like, for every 100 ms spent running uv-build to install one release of your package, Gentoo users will spend many hours building new uv-build versions over and over again.

However, build times aren’t the biggest problem; portability is. You can run Python pretty much anywhere where you can get a working C compiler. Some minor features may not work, but the core is reasonably portable. The list of platforms supported by Rust is growing slowly, and even if you can get a working Rust compiler on a given platform, uv may not work. The problems can range from bugs in the lot of packages that uv depends on (for example, rustix::fs and its dependencies skipping SPARC, for no apparent reason ), to the resulting executable being so big that the toolchain runs out of address space (and unlike system memory, you can’t really add address space to a system; the Gentoo uv ebuild already carries two hacks to make it possible to build uv on 32-bit platforms). And then, if your platform is not supported at all… well, let’s just say that adding and maintaining a new platform is a full-time job that may involve a lot of swearing at the code churn.

What about the advantages? Well, I’m aware of two reasons to use uv-build. One is consistency with using uv for your project, and it doesn’t really matter. It’s a backend and the whole point of PEP 517 is that you can use any backend with any tool. You can use flit-core, you can use hatchling , and either of them will work just fine with uv (or any other frontend). The other reason is performance and that argument makes even less sense. Even if it mattered, we’re realistically talking about a difference in the ballpark of 100 ms, for an action executed rarely; it is equally possible that any gain will be outweighed by the time needed to fetch the 1.5 MiB wheel for uv-build. But it doesn’t matter, because realistically the backend is only used by project developers, contributors, CI/CD workflows, downstream packagers and users of source distributions; all regular users use wheels instead. Of these groups, source distribution user group is the largest and the most impacted, and any performance gain is defeated by the time spent building uv-build.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI
items.content:
Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI

An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.

“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”

“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney   Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.

According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device,…

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.content:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?

items.title: Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution?
items.content:
Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution?

The last blog post I wrote explained why I chose to make FairScan open source . In particular, I said I knew there was a risk when I published FairScan's code and I was ready to accept it. I didn't expect to face that reality so soon.

What happened to me over the past few weeks

I had never heard of Ente before September 16. On that day, I received an email from one of their engineers. The message thanked me for FairScan and announced that the Ente Locker app now used FairScan's segmentation model as part of a new document scanning feature. It referred to a blog post that credited FairScan's model and claimed that Ente "wrote the image processing around it from scratch" .

I had put significant effort into FairScan's image processing so I was curious to see how Ente solved the same problems. What I found is that multiple image-processing implementations appeared to be almost direct translations of FairScan's implementations from Kotlin to Rust.

I replied by email on September 17. The engineer quickly answered that their blog post "could have been better phrased", and that it was reworded. I could see that the new version replaced the "from scratch" claim with something rather vague and still insisted on the segmentation model.

The same day, I sent a list of links to compare FairScan and Ente's code. I mentioned that I couldn't find any attribution to FairScan in the Ente repository.

On September 21, I received a reply from the same engineer that those were "fairly standard image-processing methods" and that the code had been subsequently fully rewritten. In their repository, I found a pull request affecting more than 6,000 lines . Of course, it cannot change the code that was distributed in Locker 1.0.9.

On the same day, I sent an email to copyright@ente.com to ask for the company's view on this. As of October 12, I still haven't received an answer.

On September 29, I published a post on Mastodon linking to a GitHub gist where I documented this timeline as well as code similarities .

Feel free to have a look at the code comparisons in the gist linked above and form your own opinion, even if you're not a developer. You can use the "split view" of your browser for side-by-side comparisons. Here's an example:

In the implementations I compared, I found the following similarities:

The same names for functions and variables

To me, it looks like an almost direct translation from Kotlin to Rust. There are differences but they're not easy to spot.

Of course, I have a special position about this code. I wrote it, so I know where it comes from. I know it's the result of a lot of effort:

I researched existing techniques like multi-scale Retinex, single view metrology, or gray world white balance.

I assembled an image pipeline that fits the segmentation model.

I started with some simple techniques (such as Douglas Peucker) that I later replaced.

I developed my own algorithm to approximate a quad based on contour orientation (which is probably not optimal).

I had to make choices about what a scan should look like : not all apps make the same choices.

I tested the behavior of my implementations and their parameter values on hundreds of images .

I fixed many bugs in my implementations.

I wrote blog posts about some of the numerous iterations I made, illustrating my trial and error process.

How can that be called "standard methods"? I would like to know where similar code can be found because it would have saved me a lot of work. Actually, if it already existed, I would probably not have started FairScan.

Ente has not acknowledged the code similarities as an issue , publicly or privately. In response to my comparisons, the engineer described the code as "fairly standard image-processing methods", but this didn't address the similarities I had pointed out. items.title: Mozilla launches Firefox Enterprise with self-hosted browser management
items.content:
Institutions are recalculating who controls the technology they rely on. Mozilla has an independent option to offer.

For years, organizations consolidated technology around a small number of providers to make things simpler. Fewer systems. Tighter integrations. More economies of scale. But that consolidation went well beyond technology. It consolidated dependency, too. The resulting risks have been debated, studied, and challenged along the way, but concentration continued. More work, data and critical infrastructure kept moving to the same few providers, while credible alternatives narrowed.

The deeper that dependency runs, the harder and more costly it becomes to change course. When something fails, changes or falls outside an institution’s control, that dependency becomes a risk for CIOs and CISOs to manage.

Nowhere are these stakes more visible than in Europe. Now institutions are re-assessing. Governments are pushing for greater digital autonomy, while regulated industries face growing pressure to find and manage their dependencies.

There’s a name for much of this debate about technological control: “sovereignty.”

What digital sovereignty means in practice varies. Across Europe, governments are investing in the security and resilience of critical IT infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies and putting technological autonomy higher on national agendas. Different approaches, same underlying concern. Strip away the regional policy definitions and industry distinctions and a pretty practical, universal question emerges: how much technological dependency should we risk?

And a very specific, very important layer has been largely missing from that conversation: the browser.

The browser. Applications run there. Employees authenticate in it. Sensitive data transits through it. Files are uploaded and downloaded and AI tools are increasingly used through it. That raises the same questions of dependency and control: whose browser technology are you relying on, and who controls the infrastructure used to manage it?

Firefox Enterprise is built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements. It pairs the Firefox browser, built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, with a management console organizations can run on their own infrastructure. From that console, IT teams can centrally manage browser policy and access, govern how data moves through the browser and set controls around AI use.

IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience.

“If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” said Anthony Enzor-DeMeo, CEO of Mozilla. “We built Firefox differently. And we’re bringing its independent architecture to institutions that are ready to rethink their dependencies and risk.”

We’re starting with the browser because we see it as a key, but under-governed, layer. Firefox Enterprise gives institutions more control over the browser and the infrastructure managing it.

And because Firefox runs on Gecko, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple, institutions have another path towards reducing dependence on a single architecture.

Finally, Firefox Enterprise is built to live alongside the systems that IT operations already use. Keep your identity provider. Keep your SIEM. Keep your MDM. Just add a browser whose management infrastructure you operate, so you decide where data lives and have greater visibility into how it moves.

items.title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
items.content:
Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts

Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets.

The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia.

Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.

Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions.

On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices.

The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with.

"Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said.

The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice.

“[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger .

Yesterday, Ledger provided another update , confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.”

While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware.

Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires.

The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong.

According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM.

"Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained .

Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)."

Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X.

The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan.

In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X.

"Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices.

For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.content:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that

LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree

that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion

does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields.

And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not

make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good

judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them,

interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those

One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful:

it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you

bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability,

reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we

evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does

not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false

division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs

substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each

operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually

carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying

inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should

generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool

when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise

is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain

unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a

proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop

directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what

to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a

summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading

teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question

their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to

examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does

not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's

anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire."

Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these

systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected

outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to

consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them

"conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to

do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it

cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and

delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That

distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than

declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: The ‘Sophisticated’ Bug OpenAI Found in Its Conference Room Can Be Yours for $13.99
items.content:
OpenAI said Tuesday it had sicced the FBI on an employee who was spying . But this alleged James Bond wasn’t exactly getting his tech from Q Division.

Judging from the press materials released on Tuesday by the Justice Department, the device the accused, Abdulrahman Alfozan, is said to have used to bug a conference room at an OpenAI office in San Francisco was a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense. It’s a microphone and camera the width of your thumbnail. You can order yours today for the low low price of $13.99. In a statement earlier on Tuesday, OpenAI called the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense a “sophisticated recording device.”

The Seeed website includes a YouTube video about making one into a DIY AI-pin, sort of like the ill-fated Humane Ai Pin.

Don’t get carried away imagining all the espionage fantasies that have suddenly become affordable. The $6.99 camera built into the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense is 2 megapixels, which you may remember as the resolution from the first generation iPhone. Even the disembodied AI voice in the video on the Seeed website says the images it produces is blurry.

But “sophisticated” may not be an altogether inaccurate word. The suspect was apparently (and allegedly) taking advantage of the device’s 2.4GHz Wi-Fi subsystem to transmit data to some unknown second device.

“[…]a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about ‘build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,’ ‘customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,’ ‘improv[ing] audio and live listening,’ and ‘encrypt[ing] the SD card,’ among other things.”

It seems the apparent spy was also taking video the entire time, but it was just images of the back of the conference room TV it was plugged into. The FBI claims that on October 5—well into a sort of intra-company dragnet launched by OpenAI after it found the device on September 30—Alfozan entered the bugged conference room and peeked behind the TV at his Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, inadvertently capturing this haunting selfie:

© Justice Department The Justice Department’s press release features a description of what Alfozan was allegedly up to, courtesy of FBI director Kash Patel that, if you read it a month ago, would have sounded like it was from a bad translation of a Heisei era Godzilla movie. Patel says the suspect allegedly put the device in his “employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology.”

Earlier today, OpenAI told me in an email that it used its own AI models to analyze data from the device—including forensic images of the data stored on the device—to find their suspect.

items.title: The reverts will continue until morale improves
items.content:
Many readers will be aware that an unusually high number of features

have been reverted from the PostgreSQL 19 branch after the beta period

began. Having some reverts is not unusual, maybe one per cycle could

be expected. But this time around, about 8 to 10 significant

features, depending on how you count, have been reverted, and some of

them quite late in the beta period. I have been on the receiving end

of some of that, as the developer or committer of some of those

features, and have gotten some questions about it, and so I want to

take a moment to reflect on this. I’ll try to extrapolate a little

bit to similarly affected work that I was not actively involved in,

but these are just my opinions at this point.

I don’t think we, meaning all the developers affected, have had enough

time to fully reflect on all this. But here are some thoughts. It’s

probably a combination of these, and a different combination in the

Maybe we just didn’t do a good enough job. Maybe the code was just

not good enough. We’ll learn and improve. It’s probably some of

that, and I’m mentioning it here to not give the impression that it

was only the other factors that I’m going to mention.

It could also be a coincidence. Maybe we had been on such a good

roll that we attempted to tackle several features that turned out to

be too hard, or at least too hard to finish in time.

Some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects

that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta. But there

was also a long tail of relatively harmless issues involving various

edge cases. In past times, many of these would not have surfaced

until much later and we would have fixed them bit by bit over the

subsequent five years. But with LLM-assisted code review, these

kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring

at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them

requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead

to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time. Most

if not all of the affected reverted features were written a long

time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is

now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after

the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the

capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the

current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future

A corollary of that is that, at least for the most part, as far as I

can tell, this situation is not due to “vibe coding”. This code

was written well before that was a possibility.

between, say, April (the start of feature freeze for PostgreSQL 19,

and also the start of the Vulnpocalypse) and August (the most recent

PostgreSQL security release) with working on fixes for security

issues. Because of that, the usual additional review and testing

that happens during the beta period was reduced, and then picked up

again in August. That’s possibly why a lot of new issues were

discovered quite late in the beta period and why so many reverts

happened so late, which is what made all of this so notable. Again,

some issues were more fundamental but there was also a long tail of

smaller issues, and I feel with more time, say, two months, these

could have been addressed (given adequate focus, but note that the

Vulnpocalypse is ongoing). But the community preferred trying to

Guitoro is the most realistic and the most complete virtual guitar you can play online, free in your browser. Choose a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar, an electric guitar or a four-string bass.

It's also a way to learn chords and songs that a chord chart or a video lesson can't show you. Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Then it's your turn. No guitar? Play the song on the keys or the screen, and it waits for you at every chord change. Have a guitar? Pick it up and play along at your own speed, with the strings, the strum and the fingering right in front of you.

Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument. There's nothing to download and no account to create. If you played the Google guitar doodle, Guitoro takes the idea further: six real strings, 15 chords in every key, and 51 songs to play along with.

On a phone or tablet, tap a chord pad and swipe the strings with your finger. Up to five fingers at once, and you can tap the frets on the neck to play single notes.

Drag across the strings. A fast swipe plays louder, a slow drag rolls the notes one by one, and a click plucks a single string.

On a computer, switch to Solo and every keyboard row becomes a string and every column a fret, with bends and vibrato on the arrow keys.

In a video lesson the hand moves fast and hides the strings, so you can't tell which ones were really hit. Guitar apps teach the basic chords and stop there. Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it anywhere from 20% to full speed and the chords, the strum and the band slow down together.

items.title: Fancy Curl Sites
items.content:
So a good while ago I added a fun curl version of my site, meant for viewing in the terminal. Try running these commands!

(sorry Windows users, not my fault that ANSI escape codes are disabled-by-default in cmd.exe . And not my fault that in Powershell you have to use curl.exe instead of curl because Powershell inexplicably aliases that to Invoke-WebRequest .)

I posted about it a bit on the Fediverse, but otherwise didn't elaborate much on it becuase I figured it was fairly self-explanatory. But I've had a handful of people ask me how I did it, so I decided it might actually be worth it to write a post about how I did it (…like seven months late).

I should note this idea came from trinkey's ( curl trinkey.com ) and strongsand's ( curl proot.party ) curl sites, I didn't come up with it myself. Even though I did go about it quite a bit differently from them, all credit for the very cool idea goes to them.

First, since it's the more interesting part, actually generating the ANSI-marked-up files to send to the clients. I entirely hand-wrote the index page and about page .

Note that I believe trinkey and strongsand generate theirs on-the-fly with the ratatui library (or similar), which is probably more convenient; hand-writing it seemed more expedient to me though.

I had the main escape code— ESC[ , i.e. \x1b[ — 1 in a Vim register to easily paste when needed, and then the Wikipedia page for the main graphics codes open to reference the specific escape codes. And, yeah, that's about it. I experimented to decide on consistent styling I liked, and just referenced the Gopher version of my pages when crafting the marked-up curl pages.

Now, the notable thing about my version is that I have curl versions of the entirety of my blog, rather than just one or two pages being available. This is entirely due to a convenient coincidence: over four years ago I implemented outputting ANSI-marked-up plaintext in my custom markup language I use for my blog, Gemroff . Originally it was just to allow convenient previewing of drafts in the terminal while writing; but it was trivial to plug into my static site generator to immediately get Curl versions generated.

I did manually write a wrapper template for blog posts , as well as a template for the index page listing posts , but that plus a few extra lines in my static site generator was all that was needed to wire it up.

This is the main thing that makes it hard to say it's easy! since it was only easy for me because I use an entirely custom markup language and static site generator and I happened to make the right design choices years ago—e.g. my SSG also happened to already have support for multiple, modular output formats instead of solely HTML like other SSGs, since I tri-host my site on HTTP, Gemini, and Gopher.

However, offering nothing but a few hand-written pages for fun is a completely acceptable way to set up a site like this anyways, since it's just a neat gimmick and no one's likely to actually use it more than a few minutes of browsing.

Finally, the last step is actually presenting the Curl version of your site to any user agent containing curl , which for me was just a few changes to my Nginx config , with other servers it'd presumably be equivalently simple. The main feature I wanted was an override header ( X-Original: true ) so you could still get an unmodified HTTP response like someone casually running Curl likely wanted, and I wanted everything to be served statically still.

And… that's really it! As I said, when I first set it up it seemed fairly self-explanatory to me, but it is very non-orthogonal to what people normally do with either web servers or ANSI escape codes so I can see where people's curiosity/confusion came from. It would be neat to see more sites doing this trick around!

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
items.content:
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.

In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.

You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.

Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.

The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.

Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.

Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.

China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.

Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.

In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.

Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .

Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?

In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:

Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.

The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.

The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.

From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.

People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.

items.title: Google-Tied AI Startup Once Valued at a Billion Dollars Declares Bankruptcy: Character.AI, the once-buzzy chatbot startup that faced lawsuits over the deaths of minors, has declared bankruptcy.
items.content:
Character.AI, the once-buzzy chatbot startup that faced high-profile lawsuits over the deaths of minors, has declared bankruptcy.

Character.AI announced last night that it had entered a “voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process” and is looking to sell the company in a court-supervised sale.

“Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” Character.AI said in a blog post. “After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders.”

Founded in November 2021 by then-ex-Googlers Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas, Character.AI allowed users to openly chat with a sea of largely user-generated AI companion bots known as “Characters.” It became an early success story in the frothy AI market that emerged after OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT, garnering the backing of the Silicon Valley investing juggernaut a16z and, as of March 2023 —  despite having no revenue — it was valued at more than a billion dollars. At the time, its founders spoke of the app in grandiose terms, arguing that the service would power the adoption of “personalized superintelligence.”

In September 2024, however, Shazeer, De Freitas, and dozens of other employees departed Character.AI — to rejoin Google, which threw Character.AI a $2.7 billion lifeline as part of the deal . (Shazeer now works at OpenAI .) Weeks later, Character.AI, Google, Shazeer, and de Freitas were sued by Megan Garcia , a Florida mother who alleged that her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III, died by suicide as a result of his extensive and deeply intimate interactions with chatbots on the platform. The suit, which was settled last year, sparked a wave of litigation from other families across the US claiming that their children had been abused by Character.AI, resulting in psychological harm, physical injury, and death. It was also sued by the states of Kentucky and Pennsylvania .

A huge portion of Character.AI’s userbase was kids and teens, a reality that was evident to anyone who spent time on the platform. And though the company claimed it was safe for teens aged 13 and over, Futurism investigations revealed that the supposedly safe-for-teens platform was riddled with severe content moderation issues: we found hordes of chatbots explicitly dedicated to themes of pedophilia , suicide, self-harm , and eating disorder coaching , as well as a thriving community of users creating chatbots designed to simulate school shootings , romanticize real mass shooters, and even impersonate the real child victims of mass shootings. (Character.AI even sent us automated email notifications reminding us to keep chatting with school shooter bots.)

In the wake of lawsuits and mounting safety concerns, Character.AI did make sweeping changes. It added parental controls — although they were comically easy to bypass — and moved to bar minor users from openly chatting with its chatbots. It also introduced something called “scenes,” which were brief, pre-set roleplays. (Even then, we found, “scenes” included roleplays devoted to the notorious pedophile Jeffrey Epstein .) The company’s fickle userbase didn’t love the changes .

In a court filing, Character.AI put its estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. It also said in a press release that it would sell some assets to Disney, a stalking horse bidder, for $20 million. In its blog post, the bankrupt startup stated that it hopes “the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.AI platform,” but if not, it “will be wound down.”

Character.AI is a fascinating case study of the early AI era. It was the first company to face allegations of psychological harm and wrongful death to users, claims that other major players in the industry are now battling…

items.title: Decomped Way of the Samurai 2 with fps, widescreen, high-res mods [self-promotion]
items.content:
The 2004 PS2 cult classic, decompiled and running as a real Linux and Windows program.

No emulator. No interpreter. Widescreen, any resolution, any frame rate.

Ten days in Amahara. A hungry ronin, a mute girl, a rice ball, three thugs — and

then every choice is yours. Way of the Samurai 2 never left the PlayStation 2.

This project takes the game's MIPS machine code apart function by function,

rewrites it as C++, and runs it natively: the game's own logic, its own data,

its own scripts — on your CPU, through OpenGL and SDL2.

You can play it from the title screen to the staff roll.

The whole story — all 102 story and shop scripts run on a reimplementation of the game's scripting VM, through to the endings.

Sword fighting — combos, guards, parries, the fight AI, experience and learned techniques, swords that wear down and break.

A living town — ten areas, day and night, people going about their business on the game's own task scripts.

Everything around it — shops, the inn, the blacksmith, your home, the sword safe, items, accessories, saving and loading.

Also in: the opening and ending movies, voiced dialogue with lip movement and

facial expressions, music and sound effects, the sky, water, fog, shadows,

blood, sparks and blade trails, and controller support.

A mod loader ships with three mods switched on:

Widescreen — the 3D view opens out to the sides. 16:9, 21:9, whatever shape your window is.

Resolution — draw at 1080p, 4K, or as many lines as your window has, instead of the PS2's 448.

FPS unlock — 60, 120, 144 pictures a second. The game still thinks at 30; everything in between is interpolated.

Each is a folder with an .ini you can edit. Writing your own takes one header:

replace any game file by dropping it in a folder, or load code that reads and

writes the game's memory every frame. The guide is mods/README.md .

You need your own copy of the game — the NTSC-U disc, SLUS-208.93 . Nothing

Prebuilt: download the Linux or Windows package from

start wots2 / wots2.exe . The first time it asks for your disc image. Each

# 1. Dependencies (Debian / Ubuntu / Pop!_OS)

sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build libsdl2-dev libgl-dev libarchive-dev ffmpeg

cmake -B build -G Ninja && ninja -C build

# 3. Go — hand it your disc image the first time

./build/wots2 " Way of the Samurai 2.iso "

The launcher unpacks the game's files once (into extracted/ , about 1.5 GB) and

starts the game; after that plain ./build/wots2 is enough. It takes an .iso ,

or a .zip / .7z / .rar / .tar.* holding the image or the files

themselves. Start it without an argument and it asks for the file in a window.

ffmpeg is only needed for the movies. F11 toggles fullscreen. Saves go in

SLUS_208.93 (MIPS R5900) this repository

┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐

│ game + engine code │ ───▶ │ src/game, src/engine decompiled C++ │

│ data, vtables, tables │ ───▶ │ loaded at its real PS2 addresses │

│ GS · SPU2 · pad · disc │ ───▶ │ src/hal OpenGL · SDL2 audio · input │

└─────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────────────┘

Pure decompilation. Each function is read out of Ghidra and the

disassembly and rewritten by hand. There is no MIPS interpreter anywhere.

Guest memory. The game's data is mapped at the addresses it had on the

PS2, so decompiled code and original data tables agree without translation.

Calls through vtables go through a registry of address → native function.

Hardware boundary. The Graphics Synthesizer becomes an OpenGL renderer

that records each frame as a draw list — which is what lets the same frame

be replayed wider, sharper, and in between.

About 1,900 of the binary's ~4,600 functions are decompiled. Much of the rest

is the script compiler, Sony's libraries and debug screens the game never

It plays start to finish, and automated runs take whole games through to an

ending without a crash. It is not finished:

Map and model drawing and lighting…

items.title: AOSP Source Releases Are So Late Developers Disassemble Libraries to Report Bugs
items.content:
On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character of the string that is >= U+0100 whenever the reject set has two or more characters that are all < U+0100. The character is reported as a match even though it is not in the set. wcsspn() , wcschr() , wcsrchr() , wmemchr() and wcsstr() are correct.

Any code that scans wide strings for ASCII delimiters, for example newline or wildcard characters, breaks as soon as the text contains an emoji, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek or Latin Extended character.

The public android17-release sources (android-17.0.0_r1, June 2026) build wcscspn / wcspbrk from external/llvm-libc, which is a plain nested loop over wchar_t and is correct. The code on the September builds is different (see "Mechanism"), so the regression was introduced between the June and September releases.

Build with the NDK ( aarch64-linux-android30-clang ), push to /data/local/tmp , run with adb shell :

A sweep of every code point from U+0001 to U+10FFFF (skipping surrogates and the two set members) with wcscspn(L"<cp>\n", L"x\n") returns 0 instead of 1 for 1,111,808 code points: every one from U+0100 to U+10FFFF. U+0001 to U+00FF are correct.

Which set shapes trigger it (all measured on the Pixel 8a):

Disassembly of wcscspn in /apex/com.android.runtime/lib64/bionic/libc.so on CP3A.260905.009 shows three paths selected by the set:

A character >= 0x100 cannot be in a set whose members are all < 0x100, so for wcscspn the scan must continue past it. The code stops instead. wcsspn has the same structure, and there stopping is the correct answer (the character is not in the keep set), which is why only the complement functions are wrong. wcspbrk is implemented on top of this scan and inherits the bug.

The existing bionic test TEST(wchar, wcspbrk) in tests/wchar_test.cpp only uses ASCII input, so it does not catch this. A test such as EXPECT_EQ(3u, wcscspn(L"aĀb\n", L"x\n")) would.

Visual Pinball on Android (libwinevbs, a Unix build of Wine's vbscript engine) stopped loading any table whose VBScript source contains a comment with an emoji after the September update: the lexer uses wcspbrk(ptr, L"\n\r") to skip comments, got the position of the first emoji instead of the line end, and reported "Invalid character". FileSystem.MoveFolder likewise treated every path containing a character >= U+0100 as a wildcard pattern via wcspbrk(src, L"*?><") .

Worked around downstream by replacing the calls with plain loops: vpinball/libwinevbs#41 (shipped in vpinball/vpinball@ e7837322f4 ).

Full disassembly of the affected functions and the probe sources are available on request.

items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

items.title: The AI Chatbots That Tech Companies Are Aggressively Pushing to Billions of Users Appear to Be Causing Serious Psychological Harms, New Research Finds
items.content:
A recent paper found that the extensive use of AI chatbots can be linked to “severe negative outcomes.”

According to the research , which was published in the journal JMIR Mental Health by a team of UK-based researchers at Northeastern University London and King’s College London, dark outcomes of engaging in emotional relationships with chatbots can include “addiction-like attachment, exacerbation of mental health symptoms, harmful advice,” and even “self-harm of suicidal acts.” The paper comes after extensive reporting about the public health issue known as “AI psychosis,” meaning the phenomenon in which AI users suffer delusional, paranoid , and even suicidal spirals after long-form interactions with chatbots. During these interactions, users tend to divulge extremely intimate information about their lives and mental health to their AIs, frequently turning to the products as confidantes or even therapists.

Drawing on existing research, the paper looks at AI companion bots like Replika and Character.AI, which are designed to embody specific characters, as well as general-use AI assistants like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Though emotional interactions with chatbots may provide some “potential benefits” — the authors cite “short-term reductions in loneliness and mood improvement” — they argue that any possible benefits exist alongside widely-reported “adverse outcomes” ranging from “emotional dependence” to the exacerbation of existing illnesses or symptoms to self-harm.

Among AI products’ risk factors, the researchers add, is their emotive, human-like way of engaging with users — a design choice that can result in users over-investing in a human-AI relationship that, at the end of the day, is fundamentally one-sided, according to the paper.

“Design choices that evoke personality and warmth encourage users to anthropomorphize these systems,” the paper reads, adding that “simulated empathy” can create a “structurally asymmetric interaction, in which the user discloses and the system responds, but without reciprocity, vulnerability, or accountability.”

In other words, though the relationship may feel real to the user, the authors argue, the relationship can’t be real to a chatbot.

The researchers also point to chatbot design features like agreeability and sycophancy as potentially harmful, writing that “overvalidation and sycophancy” can be a potent reinforcer of a given user’s delusional or disordered thinking, especially if a chatbot prioritizes fealty over accuracy. (In chat logs of delusional users, AI systems have been found to resist users’ attempts to reality-check their grandiose or overly-flattering claims.)

These researchers aren’t alone: their analysis follows several other studies that have flagged such features as potentially dangerous . Indeed, academics have warned since at least 2023 that chatbots could stand to reinforce delusional or disordered thought patterns , with one Google DeepMind paper from early 2024 warning that “persuasive” chatbots could negatively harm vulnerable populations, including kids, people struggling with mental illness, or those who are simply lonely. One recent study , coauthored by psychiatrists from King College London and Germany’s Protestant University of Applied Sciences, argued that the combination of sycophancy, mirrored language, and hyper-personalization may together serve as a powerful “amplification spiral” for delusional thinking in some impacted AI users.

While reporting has shown that people from all walks of life have experienced psychological harm tied to chatbot use, the paper’s authors note that not every user will be impacted in the same way.

Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context.

Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver , the region constraint rework , and more generally Project Zero . It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones.

This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high " is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit.

Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. While it looks easy to trigger, to exploit this you need an intentionally malicious Drop implementation.

I expected to see this happen: program is not accepted

Instead, this happened: program compiles and prints XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX . With asan, the program will crash with a AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope

Issue on current nightly, and stables at least down to 1.85.0

Godbolt without asan: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/GsGdqqMWe

How on earth was this not found before this???
