In 2017, a man named Michael walked onto stage in front of a packed Kresge Auditorium at MIT and attempted to draw a spiral, a common test doctors use to diagnose Parkinson’s disease. His tremors, caused by the disease, made the exercise difficult.

Then, Michael put on a wristband device made by a team of MIT students as part of 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes), who were presenting their prototype that evening.

Michael pressed a button and the device produced a subtle vibration. The vibration sent signals up his wrist and into his brain. His tremors dramatically decreased, and within seconds he was able to draw the spiral with much more precision, to a roaring ovation from the audience.

“When this device is turned on, I feel like I used to feel when I didn’t have Parkinson’s disease,” Michael told the crowd. “It’s an amazing, amazing feeling.”

The performance was so impressive that the student team received requests from classmates and others asking where they could buy the device for family and friends living with tremors. Unfortunately, the students had to explain there was only one — for the time being.

The event set off a near decade-long journey that began by leveraging MIT entrepreneurial resources like MIT Sandbox, MIT FUSE, and the MIT Venture Mentoring Service. In 2020, the student team turned into an official company, Encora Therapeutics. But there were still dozens of hardware iterations ahead. Then there were clinical trials. In one trial, 78 percent of patients reported benefits after 90 days of home use.

This February, nine years after Michael’s brave demonstration, all that work finally paid off: The FDA cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor, a condition similar to Parkinson’s that causes shaking, often in the hands.

“It’s been a long and difficult — very difficult — journey, but also very rewarding, especially when we get feedback from patients,” says Daniel Carballo ’18, SM ’20, an Encora co-founder and vice president of strategy. “We hear stories from patients about how they’ve struggled with their condition and how much they benefit from this. It reminds us why we keep going.”

The three founders of Encora who are still with the company are Carballo, Allison Davanzo ’18, and Kyle Pina ’18. They were each seniors in 2017 when they enrolled in 2.009, MIT’s popular product-design class.

The semester began with a brainstorming session in which groups of about 17 students were asked to come up with dozens of potential product ideas. Carballo proposed a wearable device that used mechanical vibration to send signals to the brain to reduce tremors. The initial idea was to help patients with Parkinson’s disease.

“It was one of hundreds of throwaway ideas,” Carballo recalls. “The initial concept was inspired by classes I had taken in robotics around neural control of movement. items.title: Announcing Lix 2.96 “Bingsu”
items.content:
We at the Lix team are proud to announce our seventh major release, version 2.96 “Bingsu”.

This release focuses on security, debugger support, quality-of-life improvements, and continues the work towards both the new Cap’n’Proto RPC protocol and Rust support.

Bingsu is a milk-based Korean shaved ice dessert with sweet toppings that may include chopped fruit, condensed milk, fruit syrup, tteok, and red beans.

Lix is a Nix implementation focused on reliability, predictability, friendliness, developed by a community of people from around the world. We have long term plans to incrementally evolve Nix to work in more places, to make it more reliable and secure, and to update the language and semantics to correct past mistakes and reduce errors, all the while providing an amazing tooling experience.

WARNING : We do not recommend to use nix upgrade-nix , please follow the instructions in https://lix.systems/install/ with the Lix’s upgrade shell script.

The upgrade procedure depends on how you installed Lix or CppNix, and is fully described in the Lix installation guide .

If you are using Lix from nixpkgs on NixOS, you just need to upgrade your nixpkgs once the upgrade pull request has passed through the build farm into your channel; no other action is required.

If you want to help us test the next version of Lix, consider running main by following the beta guide .

Lix 2.96 builds on the work of previous releases to improve the daemon, the protocols spoken with the daemon (both on a single machine and the ones used for remote builds), and brings many much-needed improvements to the debugger infrastructure.

Here’s a short list of the most exciting changes in Lix 2.96. This list is not as exhaustive as the full release notes .

Thanks to the tireless work of blokyk the REPL and debugger are much improved in Lix 2.96. The debugger is now more stable, navigating within the debugger is much easier, and the information printed by the debugger is more readable.

eldritch horrors have also switched the REPL backend from editline to rustyline , finally bringing proper UTF-8 support to the REPL.

The experimental RPC protocol is now shipping under the rpc-sockets experimental feature. As one may guess this is still highly experimental and must be enabled not only with the experimental feature flag in your Lix config, but also requires system setup that is not yet done by the NixOS module. You can find an example configuration in the NixOS module in the Lix repo .

In future releases we plan to stabilize the RPC protocol and remove support for the legacy protocols we’ve been using to date to allow further evolution of Lix.

To enable further RPC work and resolve some long-standing security inconsistencies we must remove ssh:// store URIs. Lix 2.96 deprecates ssh:// store URIs , but retains support for them without deprecation warnings. ssh:// store URI support will be removed in Lix 2.97, ssh-ng:// URIs will remain supported.

If you are using ssh:// store URIs because ssh-ng:// is missing features you need please get in touch so we can figure something out together. Note that ssh-ng has stricter security checks than ssh and no longer allows untrusted users to copy unsigned outputs to remote stores, this is intentional .

Once again Lix must break sharp corners to make improvements possible and excise surprising behavior in user code.

flake.nix validation no longer relies on poorly documented triviality checks. Instead Lix now has only one rule for flake.nix : no function calls are allowed outside of outputs . This means that Lix now accepts let blocks and string interpolation in flake inputs , among other things. We consider this a breaking change because other Nix implementations may no longer be able to evaluate Flakes that were written using Lix.

Many thanks to piegames , Qyriad and eldritch horrors .

items.title: Federal Reserve Says AI Data Center Buildout Is Making Everything More Expensive: "I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand."
items.content:
It’s not just your electricity bill that could be going up — it sounds like the massive boom in AI data centers is making practically everything more expensive.

As the Washington Post reports , officials at the Federal Reserve are starting to sing a different tune after blaming president Donald Trump’s tariff war on rising prices, admitting that the explosion in “AI-related investments” is contributing to inflationary pressures. That’s on top of Trump’s Iran war already sending the price of oil soaring.

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that AI-tied inflation is “jumping out of its lane.”

“Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said. “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.”

In economics, overheating occurs when aggregate demand outpaces productive capacity, leading to demand-side inflation, higher prices, and eventually reduced demand and consumption. In the worst case scenario, overheating can even trigger a recession .

“It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that,” Goolsbee added.

While the prices for groceries have yet to be directly impacted, economists are wondering whether it’s only a matter of time.

Worse yet, whether raising the interest rate, which makes borrowing more expensive and lowers consumer spending, will be able to meaningfully address rising inflation, is also starting to look less like a certain bet.

The Fed raised interest rates in September, the first time in three years, as inflation proves tough to beat. Futures markets expect yet another increase later this month, according to Reuters .

Meanwhile, the tens of billions of dollars being spent on AI data centers are starting to mask some fundamental problems plaguing the US economy, triggering fears over what it could look like if the AI bubble were to burst.

Sectors that have already seen instant knock-on effects from the construction boom have been consumer electronics becoming practically unaffordable, as well as a major shortage in skilled labor available for housing projects .

According to Goolsbee, “it’s clear what the Fed has to do” if inflation “remains persistent:” continue raising rates. But as tech companies show no signs of slowing down their extreme levels of spending, that lever may end up driving up the cost of investment — a reality that would make things tougher for AI companies as well.

items.title: Are Harnesses Worth the Cost?
items.content:
This article is part of the series: Exploring Gen AI.

I compared coding agents building the same API service with and without a behavioral harness. A frontier model, GPT-6 Sol, passed every external evaluation either way. But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness. While adding the harness increased token usage and runtime for Luna, the harnessed Luna runs achieved the same 10-for-10 reliability as GPT-6 Sol while costing 33% less per run ($0.273 vs $0.406). This experiment suggests a behavioral harness might be a practical way to get dependable results from smaller, cost-optimized models.

Naresh Jain is the founder of Specmatic , Xnsio and ConfEngine , and an early pioneer of the Agile movement in India. He works with software teams and engineering leaders to improve product development and technical excellence.

I went into this experiment expecting a behavioral harness to help a coding agent meet the requirements more reliably, save tokens and prevent wasted work. Giving an agent clear architectural contracts and deterministic test feedback while it coded seemed like an obvious way to help it get the implementation right on the first pass.

For GPT-6 Sol, the harness used about 10.5 times as many tokens, took nearly 3 times as long, and cost about 7 times more, yet both conditions succeeded in all 10 runs.

The results flatly contradicted that expectation and surprised me. Using Codex with GPT-6 Sol at low reasoning effort, the agent produced an application that passed all 178 automated acceptance tests in each of the 10 runs, both with and without the harness. By this measure, the harness produced no observable improvement in the final applications.

GPT-6 Sol (10-run averages for tokens, time, and cost):

The harness increased average time and cost without changing the observed acceptance result. In exploratory runs with Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (all at low reasoning effort), each also managed to complete the task unassisted on the first try.

These frontier models handled this task consistently with and without the harness. Could executable feedback help a cost-optimized model achieve similarly consistent outcomes?

Before looking at the results for a cost-optimized model, here is how I set up the experiment:

Borrowing Birgitta Böckeler’s framing , a behavioral harness combines guides and sensors . Guides anticipate where the agent might go wrong and steer it before it acts, increasing the chance of a correct first attempt. Sensors observe the results after it acts and provide feedback that helps it self-correct.

For each model, I compared agents working with and without the behavioral harness. Both conditions began with the application brief and baseline repository instructions in separate, private workspaces. Harnessed agents also received the API specifications, examples, and tools described in the inner-loop section below.

Figure 1: The two development conditions and their independent evaluation

The experiment separated development from evaluation into two distinct loops. The inner loop provided feedback to harnessed agents while they built. Once an agent finished, the outer loop ran 178 automated acceptance tests against its generated service. Both conditions faced the same evaluation, and the inner harness never had access to the evaluation suite’s answer key. Finally, I collated the accepted outcomes, token use, time, and estimated cost.

In this experiment, I treated an application as acceptable only if it started successfully and passed all 178 external acceptance tests. Reliability meant how consistently a model produced an acceptable application across repeated runs. Token use, elapsed time, and estimated cost were separate measures of run efficiency.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access

some part of my blog (Wandering Thoughts) or

CSpace , the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately

you're using a browser version that my anti-crawler precautions consider

suspicious, most often because it's too old (most often this applies to

versions of Chrome). Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague

of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM

training) that use a variety of old browser user agents, especially

Chrome user agents. To reduce the load on

Wandering Thoughts I'm experimenting with

(attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this.

If this is in error and you're using a current version of your

browser of choice, you can contact me at my current place at the

university (you should be able to work out the email address

from that). If possible, please let me know what browser you're

using and so on, ideally with its exact User-Agent string.

I am not blocking Inoreader's feed fetcher or considering it to be

too old, and it routinely fetches feeds from me. I don't know why

Inoreader is showing you this page. It is possible that they're

periodically trying to fetch feeds or pages with an old browser

HTTP User-Agent (or an actual old browser) and taking the results

of that fetch (this page) as what they should show people instead

of the results of their syndication feed fetcher agents. This is a

of modern HTTP fetches depend partly on the HTTP User-Agent used .

Much like Inoreader, Feedly is periodically fetching my syndication

feeds with a fake, old browser HTTP User-Agent header, which fails,

and is then grimly latching on to the results for their actual feed

fetching with their regular Feedly HTTP User-Agent. There is nothing

I can do about this; you should contact Feedly support, if you can

comment of mine in Wandering Thoughts for more details.

Due to an ongoing attack, you may need to change

"User Agent Brand Masking" setting so that your Vivaldi identifies

itself as Vivaldi, instead of Google Chrome. This applies to even

You may be seeing this through archive.today, archive.ph, archive.is,

and so on. Unfortunately, archive.* crawls pages to archive in a way that

is impossible to distinguish from malicious actors. They use old Chrome

User-Agent values, crawl from IP address blocks that are widely distributed

and not clearly identified as theirs, and some of their IP addresses have

falsified reverse DNS entries that claim they are googlebot IP addresses

(which is something that is normally done only by quite bad actors). I

suggest that you use archive.org, which is a better behaved archival

crawler and can crawl my blog (Wandering Thoughts) .

items.title: Drone strikes didn’t take out a Russian bot farm, but we were primed to believe it
items.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to journalists after meeting with the German chancellor in Kyiv on October 4. Volodymyr Tarasov/Ukrinform/Zuma

Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily .

On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that a Ukrainian bombing strike on Yandex’s data centers, a large Russian technology company, had led to a sudden decrease in bot activity online. “When our strikes reached Yandex’s data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms,” Zelenskyy declared, speaking at the opening of the Warsaw Security Forum. There was, he added, “less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots. And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from.”

The claim quickly picked up speed, and gained specificity: that following the Ukrainian strikes, all kinds of internet users were suddenly less present online, including MAGA accounts, those supporting Reform UK, and ones supporting AfD, the German ultra-right party. A Polish political scientist shared claims that bot activity supporting AfD had dropped by 56 percent, a post that was viewed millions of times and has since been deleted. As Radio Free Europe has reported, a Czech politician shared a similar claim, writing, “So much talk about German patriotism…then the connection from Russia goes down.”

The underlying claim, in other words, was that a great deal of political activity online across a number of countries is inauthentic and led by Russian bots. Their sudden alleged silencing was a simple, feel-good story amidst the endless fight against online disinformation .

“I’m sorry to burst everyone’s bubble, but as of now, there is no solid evidence that Russian bot farms have become inactive.”

The only problem was that it simply wasn’t true.

Tech experts quickly explained that the “bots” that had been taken offline by the Yandex strike were actually bot crawlers, also known as web crawlers, which continually browse the internet in order to index web pages. A widely circulated chart from Cloudflare, the infrastructure company, did indeed show a drop in traffic from Yandex’s servers, which made sense; both the company’s web crawlers and search index requests were disrupted by the bombing campaign.

The first issue, then, was the word “bot,” which “means different things in different contexts, which is contributing to some public confusion,” explains Renee DiResta . She’s an associate research professor at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy, a social media researcher, and a globally recognized expert on disinformation. “It is used as shorthand for both web crawlers and online trolls. Web crawlers plummeting makes sense, but online trolls usually have more resilient infrastructure.”

The second problem, however, was that the ultra-specific claims about less activity in certain areas—MAGA, pro-Kremlin bot accounts, and AfD—had absolutely no basis in fact.

“We see no “dramatic drop” in traffic of Kremlin-aligned human trolls-for-hire targeting Russian domestic users (which we have been tracking for years),” wrote Antibot4Navalny , a group of anonymous researchers who track and respond to Russian disinformation.

Participants in one study tended to “overestimate the prevalence of bots and see others as more vulnerable to bot influence than themselves.”

Proton multiplie les services, au risque de ressembler de plus en plus à Google. Et certains grincent des dents, même si l'entreprise, elle, assume parfaitement sa stratégie. Navigateur, messagerie mobile, et pourquoi pas un téléphone ? Pour le fondateur Andy Yen, certaines choses sont inévitables pour rester compétitif.

Navigateurweb , alternative à Signal, Proton Phone : « Tout ça est inévitable » – Interview Andy Yen

Cet été, une simple offre d'emploi pour un ingénieur Chromium a suffi à relancer les spéculations sur un éventuel navigateur signé Proton. De son côté, la communauté s'interroge déjà sur la multiplication des produits de l'entreprise. Nous avons donc posé la question à son patron, Andy Yen, avant d'aborder l'avenir des standards du web, les chances de voir arriver une messagerie alternative à Signal, mais aussi les lacunes basiques de cet écosystème grandissant.

Vous avez embauché un ingénieur logiciel expérimenté sur la plateforme Chromium. Pouvez-vous clarifier votre position sur un navigateur web et votre avis sur Gecko, le moteur de Firefox ?

Andy Yen : Ce que les gens reprochent à Chromium, au fond, c'est Google, non ? Si on retire Google de l'équation, c'est en réalité du très bon code. Le risque, c'est de se demander ce qui se passera si Google décide un jour, pour une raison ou une autre, d'y ajouter toujours plus de choses, de le polluer, d'en arrêter la maintenance ou de le rendre plus difficile à exploiter pour les autres navigateurs. Beaucoup de personnes qui n'utilisent pas un navigateur basé sur Chromium affirment que, si Google changeait ses politiques, tous les éditeurs ayant adopté la plateforme en subiraient les conséquences.

Si je suis moins pessimiste, c'est que je vois suffisamment d'acteurs construire par-dessus Chromium. Si Google décidait un jour de le rendre inutilisable pour tous les autres, je pense qu'une communauté assez large se mobiliserait pour rendre un fork possible.

Proton aurait pu sauver Mozilla et Firefox, mais a plié devant Chromium 10 août 2026 à 08h47

Je comprends votre point de vue, mais il y a aussi un revers : plus on pousse Chromium, plus c'est Google qui finit par fixer les standards du web. Et on se doute bien que l'entreprise fait évoluer ces standards en fonction de ses propres intérêts.

A.Y : Mais du coup, c'est surtout un problème de standards ouverts du web, vous ne trouvez pas ? C'est la discussion que nous avons toujours avec Sir Tim, le W3C et les autres. Dans une certaine mesure, cette bataille est perdue depuis longtemps, pour être tout à fait honnête.

A.Y : Oui, je pense que cette bataille est déjà perdue. La seule façon de changer l'avenir, c'est qu'il y ait plus d'une ou deux entreprises dominantes. Aujourd'hui, qui contrôle le W3C et tout cet écosystème ? Google, Apple, peut-être un tout petit peu Microsoft ici et là, et, loin derrière, éventuellement Amazon. Mais c'est principalement Google. Tant qu'un autre Google n'aura pas émergé pour contester cette position, je ne pense pas que le statu quo change vraiment. C'est avant tout une question de puissance économique et de distribution.

Vous m'avez déjà interviewé il y a dix ans, et quand vous m'interviewerez à nouveau dans dix ans, nous serons alors dans une autre position : Proton sera plus grand, nous aurons réussi notre mission et nous pourrons rivaliser. Mais pour l'instant, se dire « je vais soutenir ces autres projets juste pour maintenir de la diversité », c'est ce que les anglophones appellent « pissing into the fire », un peu l'équivalent de notre « pisser dans un violon ». Ça ne changera rien, malheureusement.

Toujours à propos du navigateur, quel serait l'objectif aujourd'hui ? Un navigateur similaire à Brave, ou plutôt axé sur des agents intelligents ?

A.Y : Tout le monde a supposé que nous construisions un navigateur parce qu'une offre d'emploi est apparue, mais ce n'est pas nécessairement le cas. Nous faisons énormément de choses liées au web chez Proton, et il y a plein de…

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
